19775-vaughan-s-vegetable-cook-book-4th-:
Vaughan's Vegetable Cook Book, in its fourth edition, teaches cooking and using vegetables. Its guidance runs from soil to table. One passage covers forcing heads of leafy crops under manure-warmed soil. Fresh manure twelve inches thick, it advises, warms the bed slightly. That warmth hastens the making of the head. Vaughan's was a Chicago seed house serving home gardeners.

Cookbooks from seed firms doubled as garden manuals. Recipes sold seeds, and growing notes sold recipes. A fourth edition proves steady demand for both. The book preserves period varieties and period tastes together. Kitchen historians can trace how vegetables were raised and served. Few sources tie the garden bed to the dinner plate so directly.
19819-milton-s-comus:
John Milton wrote Comus, a masque, in 1634, when he was twenty-five. This edition, prepared by William Bell, adds an introduction and notes. Bell quotes Walter Bagehot's high estimate of the poem. Bagehot doubted any similar poem shows so well the mind's dignity. He found its sentiments tedious and its story uninteresting, yet praised it anyway. That tension shapes Bell's school edition.

Comus defends chastity and temperance in enchanted-wood scenes. A school edition must make its poetry teachable. Notes explain myth, language, and Milton's life. Bagehot's mixed verdict models honest criticism for students. The masque's music and moral argument still reward slow reading. Bell's volume shows Victorian schools keeping Milton central.
20181-a-defective-santa-claus:
A Defective Santa Claus, from 1904, is a Christmas tale told in lively dialect verse. Uncle Sid clucks, leans back laughing, and waves the sleigh away. He yells that the old horse ought to wear bells by now. Pa yells back that bells can wait till Santa comes this way.

Such verse tales ran in papers and gift books each December. Dialect spelling gives the jokes their rural, Hoosier-style flavor and bounce. Family, snow, and a flawed Santa drive the fun along. Readers get a short, warm dose of old Christmas humor in rhyme.
20732-the-carmina-of-caius-valerius-catu:
Catullus, a Roman poet of the first century before Christ, wrote short, fierce, and tender poems called the Carmina. The notes here grew in an odd way, drafted at a hotel table between courses. A Latin text sat open while talk went on around the writer.

Readers get love poems, insults, jokes, and grief in quick turns. Catullus can sound sweet in one line and brutal in the next. His voice feels startlingly modern across two thousand years. This edition pairs the poems with lively notes that show a reader working through the Latin line by line, with real delight.
20981-tristram-of-blent-an-episode-in-th:
A club man who once quit the Bar for letters fills Tristram of Blent's opening talk. He edits, not writes, by his own cheerful account of his trade. Anthony Hope sets this 1900 tale in an ancient house's long story.

Imposture, inheritance, and a fine old place drive Hope's polished plot. The true heir and a bold stand-in circle the Tristram name and lands. Hope, famed for The Prisoner of Zenda, writes with speed and sheen. This tale shows his lighter hand at work on English soil, with secrets in every portrait-hung room.
21858-the-daughters-of-danaus:
Marriage and a woman's right to her own growth are fought over in Mona Caird's The Daughters of Danaus, first published in 1894. The tale opens in a garret ballroom in an old keep, where dancers move to a reel in the moonlight. Celtic music sets nerves athrill even in the low-key scene. Caird's Scotland is wild, old, and full of pressure on its women.

An appendix prints Caird's own essay asking whether marriage hinders a woman's self-development. She had already scandalized Victorian readers by calling marriage a failure in print. The novel gives her argument flesh and landscape. It stands as one of the boldest feminist novels of the 1890s, still startling in its plain refusal of women's lot.
21909-a-military-genius:
Anna Ella Carroll of Maryland is called the great unrecognized member of Lincoln's Cabinet in this 1891 life by Sarah Ellen Blackwell. Blackwell compiled the book from family records and congressional documents. She had hoped Carroll herself would oversee the statements, but the family decided otherwise. The claim at the book's heart is bold: that Carroll, a woman, supplied key military thinking for the Union cause.

Carroll moved in Maryland politics and wrote pamphlets for the Union when her state wavered. Blackwell argues her plans reached Lincoln's war councils without public credit. The book was sold at the Woman's Journal office and suffrage rooms. It is at once a biography and a brief for women's uncounted public work, argued from papers her subject's family kept.
22004-the-genius:
Margaret Potter's novel The Genius came out in 1906, after her books Istar of Babylon and The House of De Mailly. The action opens on New Year's night in 1840, in the Russian town of Klin. Snow, church bells, and the old calendar set the scene. From there the tale follows a gifted young Russian as he grows up under the Czar's rule.

Chapters carry him through the Corps of Cadets, first love, and the Moscow Conservatoire. Music becomes the centre of his life, yet the secret police, the Third Section, watch men like him closely. Potter mixes court balls, camp life, and student folly with a darker strain of fate. The result is a big, earnest story of talent tested by power.
22270-bloom-of-cactus:
Robert Ames Bennet published Bloom of Cactus in 1919, a western novel of the Arizona desert. Its frontispiece shows Lennon raising his rifle to fire a parting shot over fleeing riders' heads. Lennon lingers on a ridge to enjoy the glorious view while his burro, uninterested in scenery, plods down the far trail. The desert light, not the animal, holds the man.

Bennet peoples the cactus country with prospectors, raiders, and a girl worth the title's bloom. Gunplay and desert craft move the plot in the pulp-western manner. Bennet wrote many such tales of the border country. This one keeps his formula: a hard land, a cool hero, and romance flowering where nothing should grow.
22521-the-young-acrobat-of-the-great-nor:
The Young Acrobat of the Great North American Circus promises big-top adventure. Its circus bills itself as an unparalleled show of many attractions. Never, the puff claims, has it embraced a greater variety.

World-famous acrobats headline the bill in large numbers. Clowns, bareback riders, and rope walkers fill out the ring. Trapeze artists and star performers complete the human cast. A colossal menagerie adds elephants, tigers, and lions. Leopards and other wild animals appear in great variety too. Behind that glitter stands the young acrobat of the title. His story takes readers inside circus life. Period boys read such books with sawdust in their dreams.
22875-circus:
A fall starts the trouble in Circus, a story told in the first person. The narrator broke no bones but was shaken up and left limping. The fall happened near the highway to the George Washington Bridge. From there he tried to flag down a ride, and his troubles found their road.

The circus of the title waits ahead of that roadside opening, with its own world of performers and risk. The telling stays plain and close, like a man recounting the strangest stretch of his life. Injury, travel, and the show business of big tops and small towns mix in the pages. Readers who like offbeat American storytelling will find a curious, grounded little narrative here.
22955-the-mistakes-of-jesus:
Bold questions drive The Mistakes of Jesus, a work of religious criticism dated 1932. Suppose a critic declares that Jesus lacked the highest intelligence. How, the book asks, can the critic be sure of his own judgment? How do you know your appraisal is right, lest you be found to fight against God? The author takes that challenge head-on rather than dodging it.

Page by page, the text examines sayings and actions of Jesus and judges them by reason and ethics. Believers of its day found the book shocking, and it was printed for a freethought readership that prized plain speaking. Its value now is historical as much as argumentative. It shows how far public criticism of scripture had come by the early twentieth century.
a-kidnapped-santa-claus: A short Christmas tale by L. Frank Baum in which the wicked Daemons of the caves plot to ruin the holiday by kidnapping Santa Claus. With Saint Nick locked away, his helpers must save Christmas Eve themselves. alvira-the-heroine-of-vesuvius: A. J. O'Reilly's novel about Alvira, heroine of Vesuvius: romance and adventure beneath the volcano. anti-federalist-papers-brutus:
The Brutus essays, sixteen in all, ran in New York papers across 1787 and 1788 against ratifying the Constitution. Brutus is thought to be Robert Yates, a New York judge and delegate who left the Philadelphia convention. The essays are the weightiest work of the Anti-Federalist side.

Brutus warns that a vast republic cannot stay free, and that the new federal courts and tax powers would crush the states. He predicts the Senate, the presidency, and the judiciary would drift into an aristocracy. The Bill of Rights owes much to pressure from Brutus and his allies. His losing side still frames American debates on federal power.

euthydemus: Plato's comic dialogue pits Socrates against two sophist brothers who can prove anything, including that Socrates is his own father. fables-for-the-frivolous: Guy Wetmore Carryl takes Aesop's fables and turns them deliciously upside down in witty verse. father-sergius: Tolstoy's haunting late story about Prince Kasatsky, who becomes the holy hermit Father Sergius only to find pride and desire waiting in the wilderness. govdocs-archive_org-nsia-PaulingLinus_Pa: A research note dated April 7, 1973 concerns a quotation about insanity attributed to Linus Pauling. govdocs-archive_org-nsia-PostalServiceUS:
The Bureau of Chief Postal Inspector issued this final report in September 1968. Its subject is the mailing of firearms under allegedly fictitious names. Mail-order guns moved through the postal system under names that inspectors believed were invented, and the bureau investigated the practice as a system, not a single case.

The Oswald rifle had been bought by mail under the name A. J. Hidell, which made this subject a live one for years after Dallas. A 1968 report shows the Post Office still working the problem at full scale. It records the bureau's findings on how fictitious-name orders were placed and what could be done about them. For readers, it is the administrative sequel to a famous purchase.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WatergateManusc: Harold Weisberg turned from the Kennedy case to Watergate in a set of manuscript pages. The draft covers G. govdocs-archive_org-oswald-spengler-hera: Oswald Spengler, the German historian known for The Decline of the West, wrote a study of Heraclitus, the early Greek thinker. Heraclitus taught that all things flow and change, and only fragments of his words survive. The edition includes a foreword by Rodolfo Mondolfo on how to interpret him. Spengler reads the fragments as one mind's whole view of the world, not as scattered sayings.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_afghanis:
As the Soviet war in Afghanistan wound down in the late 1980s, four powers circled the country's future. A New Phase in the Great Game follows the United States, the Soviets, India, and Pakistan as each tried to shape a new Afghanistan.

The Great Game was the old name for rivalry over Central Asia, and the briefing book argues it never really ended. Declassified records show diplomats and intelligence services backing clients and blocking rivals while Afghans bore the cost. The collection serves readers who want the end of the Soviet war told from the files of all four capitals.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_china_Ch: China's Tibet Problem: The Contentious History - the National Security Archive briefing-book page capture. The archivists capture, complete. A single capture. Dated material, filed. From the archive's collection, for researchers of the records and readers.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_intellig:
In the 1950s the Soviet missile program was a hard target for American intelligence, meaning a secret very hard to penetrate. James E. David edited this briefing book, number 695, published in February 2020. It covers United States efforts against that program through 1957.

The failures are candid. Washington learned of the first Soviet ICBM test from a Soviet press release. News of the second came from a remark made to a French politician. Sputnik's launch caught the United States unaware until the satellite was in orbit. The record shows an intelligence system learning, expensively and in public, how much it did not know.

For sixty-five years the United States has tracked objects in orbit, building a space surveillance network to watch an ever more crowded sky. James E. David and Charles Byvik edited this briefing book, number 824, published in March 2023. Its title asks the network's three basic questions.

What is up there, where is it, and what is it doing: that is the daily work of cataloging satellites and debris. The documents span the effort from the early space age to today's congestion. Readers get the unglamorous backbone of space power, the tracking that makes both military planning and collision warnings possible.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nuclear-: Castle BRAVO, detonated at Bikini Atoll in 1954, yielded far more power than its designers predicted and spread fallout over inhabited islands and a Japanese fishing boat. This briefing-book page marks seventy years since that shot, which its title calls the worst nuclear test in United States history. The evidence supplied here is the title alone, and the test documents are not described. BRAVO's legacy includes sick Marshall Islanders, a dead fisherman, and the modern politics of nuclear testing compensation.

Twice in 1979 and 1980, American warning systems reported Soviet missile attacks that were not happening, and United States forces went on alert. This briefing-book page presents the record of those false warnings. A companion Archive volume on Colonel Odom's four a.m. phone call covers the same alert system in detail. The evidence here is the title alone. The episodes remain the standard cautionary case in nuclear safety: minutes of confusion, inside a system built to react in minutes.

The United States Air Force filmed its own preparations for nuclear war, and some of that film has been declassified. William Burr edited this briefing book, posted in March 2023, built around those movies. One shows the crew of an American bomber at work.

Evidence here is short, so description stays plain. Films made for training and morale show nuclear war as a job: checklists, uniforms, calm voices. That ordinariness is the historical point. Moving images of crews rehearsing the end of the world reveal how completely the mission had been normalized inside the service that would fly it.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_southern:
Argentine generals seized power on March 24, 1976, opening seven years of military rule and mass repression. Briefing Book number 752, edited by Carlos Osorio and published in March 2021, asks a narrower question: what did the United States know before the coup, and when did it know it?

The documents show American officials had ample warning that a coup was being plotted, and kept a channel open to the plotters themselves. The Ford administration knew the military planned grave abuses against human rights. One episode stands out: the American ambassador stopped a pre-coup visit by a former deputy director of the CIA. For readers, the papers shift blame from surprise to choice, showing a government informed early and engaged anyway.
grass-of-parnassus: Poems by Andrew Lang, the fairy-tale collector, showing his other talent: light, learned verse on books, old songs, and lost worlds. Graceful and nostalgic, they are the work of a scholar who never lost his sense of play. A pleasant volume from a many-sided man of letters.
greek-romances-heliodorus-longus-achille:
Rowland Smith translated three surviving Greek novels of love and adventure in one volume. Heliodorus wrote the Ethiopics, Longus wrote Daphnis and Chloe, and Achilles Tatius wrote Clitopho and Leucippe. All three date from the Roman imperial centuries.

Lovers are separated by pirates, storms, false deaths, and jealous rivals. Heliodorus opens in mid-action and unwinds his plot backward with great skill. Longus tells a gentler tale of two foundlings growing into love on Lesbos. Achilles Tatius favors lush description and narrow escapes. Together these romances show the ancient novel learning to entertain at length.
holberg-comedies-by-holberg-jeppe-of-the:
Ludvig Holberg, often called the Danish Moliere, wrote the three comedies gathered here in English. Jeppe of the Hill wakes a drunken peasant as a lord for a day. The Political Tinker mocks a craftsman who thinks he can run the state. Erasmus Montanus skewers a student drunk on Latin learning.

Each play turns one human folly into laughter with a kind edge. Peasants, burghers, and scholars all get their turn under Holberg's whip. The jokes still land because pride and pretence have not changed. These plays founded a stage tradition in Scandinavia and remain its comic bedrock.
josephus:
Josephus is Norman Bentwich's study of the ancient Jewish historian, published at Philadelphia in 1914. Bentwich had already written on Philo-Judaeus of Alexandria. Nine chapters run from The Jews and the Romans to a conclusion. A bibliography, a list of abbreviations, and an index support the text.

Two chapters follow Josephus's life to the fall of Jotapata and after his surrender to Rome. Others treat his works, his relation to earlier writers, and the Jewish Wars. Bentwich also sets Josephus beside the Bible and later Jewish history. A final chapter reads his apology as a defense of Judaism. The book introduces a writer whose histories remain a chief source for his age.
lives-of-girls-who-became-famous:
Sarah Knowles Bolton wrote these lives for aspiring girls in 1914. She had earlier written Poor Boys Who Became Famous. Her preface insists life is earnest activity, not a play-day. Goethe and Jean Ingelow supply mottoes about energy and work.

Bolton offers George Eliot and Rosa Bonheur as grand examples. Elizabeth Fry visited the poor and the prisoner instead. Mrs. Stowe and Miss Alcott lightened their parents' burdens by writing. Rich readers, like Baroness Burdett-Coutts, must bless the world generously. Mary Lyon's persistency shows poor girls what purpose can accomplish. Work is heaven's hest, Jean Ingelow's quoted line declares.
maitre-cornelius:
Maitre Cornelius is a tale by Honoré de Balzac, in Katharine Wormeley's translation. It opens on All Saints' Day, 1479, in the cathedral of Tours. Vespers are ending, and darkness fills the unfinished towers. Archbishop Hélie de Bourdeilles rises to bless the faithful.

In that candlelit gloom Balzac sets his medieval mystery. Cornelius is the aged treasurer and moneylender of King Louis XI. His hoarded gold and secret house draw young lovers into danger. A young nobleman risks all to reach the girl he loves. Balzac blends history, romance, and his great theme of money. The tale is the Human Comedy's medieval chapter.
mediaeval-lore-from-bartholomew-anglicus:
Robert Steele gathered Mediaeval Lore from Bartholomew Anglicus, with a preface by William Morris. Bartholomew was an English friar of the 1200s who wrote a vast store book. Steele picks its most curious entries for modern readers.

Morris opens by fighting the old view of the middle ages. That age, he says, was no mere chaos between two bright eras. He credits new study of history and art for the change. The lore itself ranges over beasts, plants, stones, and the skies. A picture of thinkers on Mount Olympus fronts the book. Keats lines on holy air and water set its mood.
menexenus:
Menexenus is a short dialogue attributed to Plato, presented here in Benjamin Jowett's translation. In it, Socrates recites a funeral oration over Athens's war dead. He claims, with a straight face, that Aspasia taught it to him. The speech praises Athens in the grand style of public oratory.

Jowett's appendix, printed with the text, weighs doubts about which Platonic works are genuine. Funeral speeches, he notes, are exactly the kind of writing most open to forgery. He explains how unknown works easily gained a famous author's name. Read together, speech and appendix raise sharp questions about rhetoric, patriotism, and authorship.
moon-of-israel-a-tale-of-the-exodus:
H. Rider Haggard set this tale of the Exodus in ancient Egypt, narrated by the scribe Ana. His author's note argues a bold thesis about Pharaoh. The real Pharaoh of the Exodus, he suggests, was the usurper Amenmeses. Amenmeses held the throne briefly between Meneptah and Seti II, and his body has never been found.

Chapters move from Tanis to the land of Goshen, with the breaking of a cup and a prophecy. Seti counsels Pharaoh, Amon is smitten, and the Nile runs red. Haggard meant to dedicate the book to Egyptologist Gaston Maspero, who died during the war. The note adds the dedication at his family's wish.
mucedorus:
Mucedorus is an old stage comedy of love and danger in two kingdoms. Its full title names Prince Mucedorus of Valencia and Amadine of Aragon. The cast lists kings, nobles, a maid, and councillors. Scenes move between courts and a wild forest.

The catalog credits the play to William Shakespeare, as old editions did. V1 notes it was acted by his company and loved in its day. A prince in disguise seeks the princess he loves. A wild man of the woods adds threat and fun. Scholars still debate who wrote it, which makes this popular romance a neat puzzle of the early stage.
nasa-tm-19650019798-rocket-motor-spin-te:
Robert L Swain, Melvin H Lucy, and Peter H Foss at Langley described a spin-test rig for solid rocket motors in October 1964. Some motors behave differently while spinning in flight. Burning and gas flow inside the motor can change under spin. Hot residue can also settle in new places, raising the risk of failure.

Their apparatus subjects a motor to spin or roll while it is tested on the ground. That lets engineers reproduce flight conditions safely. The paper was given at a static testing meeting in California. Ground spin tests offered a way to find spin-related faults before a motor ever flew.
nasa-tm-19700011382-sound-measurements-o:
Loren W. Acker, Joseph R. Balombin, and James W. Coats of the Lewis Research Center wrote this report in March 1970. They measured the sound made by a high-bypass turbofan engine. The engine gave four thousand pounds of thrust in the tests.

Sound data were taken at several engine speeds. The team also varied the nozzle areas of the fan and the core engine. One strong single tone stood out above the rest of the noise, they found. It matched the rate at which the fan blades passed a fixed point. The report gives the noise levels that listeners would perceive at those settings.
nasa-tm-19720014944-precipitation-criter:
Glenn E Daniels of the Marshall Space Flight Center wrote these precipitation guidelines on March 22, 1972, as NASA TM X-64650. Daniels worked in the Aero Astrodynamics Laboratory. Rockets and spacecraft must survive rain while waiting and launching. Designers need agreed extremes of rainfall to build against. This document supplies those numbers for NASA vehicle development. It pairs with his broader climate criteria work.

The guidelines give likely extremes and traits of precipitation. Rainfall rate chances form the core of the data. Drop size and the speed at which drops fall are included. Wind speeds that come with rain also matter for loads on a waiting vehicle. Associated equipment falls under the same guidance. Weather criteria like these quietly shape launch site rules.
nautilus:
Laura E. Richards published Nautilus in Boston in 1895, and this copy marks the tenth thousand printed. Estes and Lauriat issued it, with pictures. Richards had already written Captain January and Melody. She dedicated the story to the Howe Club of Gardiner, Maine.

Early chapters meet the boy John, then a skipper, then a great exhibition. John goes aboard the Nautilus, and a chapter named Mystery follows. The chapter heads alone promise a sea tale for young readers, built around a boy and a ship. Richards writes with warmth, and the sea setting gives the story its pull.
old-scores-and-new-readings-discussions-:
John Runciman wrote these essays on music and musicians. The book appeared in London in the year 1901. The contents begin with William Byrd and his Mass. Henry Purcell is called our last great musician. Bach, Handel, Haydn, and Mozart receive long essays.

Later pieces treat Schubert, Weber, Wagner, and Verdi. Famous operas such as Tristan and Lohengrin are discussed. Runciman gives firm, personal judgments on each composer. He asks readers to hear old scores with fresh ears. The book suits music lovers who enjoy strong opinions. Its essays span four centuries of European music.
peck-s-bad-boy-with-the-circus: The sample hosted for this entry shows only the front matter of Peck's Bad Boy with the Circus, the title pages and contents, with no chapter text visible. phaedrus: Plato's dialogue on love and rhetoric, set by a stream outside Athens. Socrates' great speech on the soul as a charioteer, and his critique of writing itself, make this one of his most beautiful works. Philosophy as poetry.
philebus: Plato's dialogue on pleasure versus wisdom: which makes the better life? Socrates argues for a measured mix, with reason in charge. Subtle, complex, and rewarding, it is his deepest treatment of the good life. The argument is dense but the prize is great: Plato's fullest answer to what makes a life worth living.
poems-patriotic-religious-miscellaneous: The poems of Abram Joseph Ryan, the "poet-priest of the Confederacy": "The Conquered Banner" and other verses of faith and Southern memory. Fervent, musical, and deeply felt, they made him beloved in the South. The voice of a lost cause.
polly-of-the-circus: Margaret Mayo's beloved 1907 play about Polly, a bareback rider in a traveling circus, who falls for the young minister who disapproves of her world. Sentiment, spectacle, and a clash between sawdust and sanctimony made it a huge Broadway success. This edition preserves one of the era's most popular melodramas.
quaint-gleanings-from-ancient-poetry-a-c: Antiquarian Edmund Goldsmid gathered odd and charming bits of old verse that had fallen out of fashion. The collection offers curious rhymes, forgotten ballads, and playful poems from centuries past, chosen for their strangeness as much as their beauty. Browsers will find it a cabinet of literary curiosities, full of small surprises from the poetry of earlier ages.

tanakh-jps-1917-exodus: Slavery in Egypt, a baby hidden in a basket, and a burning bush: the story of Moses begins here. Exodus follows the Israelites from bondage through ten plagues, across the parted Red Sea, to Mount Sinai, where they receive the Ten Commandments. The 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation presents this founding story of liberation in the first English rendering by Jewish scholars.
tanakh-jps-1917-leviticus: Priests, sacrifices, and the rules of holy living fill this law book, the third of the five books of Moses. Leviticus sets out offerings, dietary laws, festivals, and the Day of Atonement, when the high priest sought forgiveness for the whole people. This 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation brings the ancient Hebrew ritual code into English for the first time by a Jewish scholarly committee.

the-age-of-big-business-a-chronicle-of-t: Hendrick’s chronicle of the tycoons’ age, from Rockefeller to Carnegie and beyond. He shows how big business built modern America. Trusts, rails, and steel fill these busy pages. The captains of industry, warts and all.
the-complete-works-of-artemus-ward-part-: Part seven of Artemus Ward's complete works: the miscellaneous pieces. Leftover gems from America's first humorist. The showman's final drolleries. the-gathering-of-brother-hilarius: A medieval tale by Michael Fairless about Brother Hilarius, a young monk who leaves his monastery and learns holiness from the world outside. Gentle, devout, and beautifully written, it follows his wanderings among the poor and simple. Published in 1901, it is a small classic of spiritual fiction, loved by readers seeking quiet wisdom.
the-life-and-adventures-of-santa-claus: L. Frank Baum, author of The Wizard of Oz, gives Santa Claus a full origin story. A human baby is found in the forest and raised by immortals, grows up loving children, and begins delivering hand-carved toys on Christmas Eve, earning the title of Saint. Baum's 1902 book mixes fairy-tale whimsy with real tenderness, and it quietly shaped how America pictures Santa today.
the-lives-of-the-twelve-caesars-volume-0: The Roman biographer Suetonius profiles Augustus, the first emperor of Rome, in this ancient account written about a century after his death. Readers meet the shrewd young Octavian who ended a hundred years of civil war and rebuilt Rome in marble. Gossipy, vivid, and packed with telling detail, it remains our most colorful source on the man who created the Roman Empire.

Augustus's successor Tiberius was a brilliant general who became a bitter, reclusive emperor. Suetonius recounts his retreat to the island of Capri and the dark rumors that followed him there — stories of cruelty and debauchery that may say as much about Rome's gossip as about the man. A haunting portrait of power curdling into paranoia.

Claudius was the unlikely emperor — mocked for his stammer and limp, yet he conquered Britain and ruled ably for thirteen years. Suetonius gives us a man dominated by his wives, ending with the famous suspicion that Agrippina poisoned him to make way for Nero. History's great underdog emperor, in all his strange contradictions.

Of all Rome's short-lived emperors, Vitellius is remembered as the glutton — a man Suetonius says cared more for feasts than for governing. Seizing power in the chaos of 69 AD, he was dragged through Rome and executed within months. A grotesque, almost comic figure whose biography reads like a warning about appetite unrestrained.
the-lives-of-the-twelve-caesars-volume-1: Titus earned the title delight of mankind — the emperor who finished the Colosseum and won his people's love. Yet Suetonius reminds us he was also the general who destroyed Jerusalem. Ruling barely two years before his sudden death in 81 AD, he remains one of history's most appealing might-have-beens, glowing all the brighter for his brief reign.
the-roman-pronunciation-of-latin-why-we-: Frances Lord explains the Roman pronunciation of Latin — why scholars use it and how teachers should teach it — in this clear school manual. Her practical guidance settled many a classroom dispute. A useful little book, still handy for Latin teachers.
theaetetus: Plato's dialogue on knowledge: what is it to know something? Socrates tests definitions with the young Theaetetus, ending in noble failure. Brilliant, honest, and foundational, it is the first great work on epistemology. No final answer emerges, but the search itself becomes a model of honest thinking.
thoughts-of-marcus-aurelius: The Meditations of Marcus Aurelius — Roman emperor and Stoic philosopher — gather his private reflections on duty, mortality, and the good life. Written in Greek on military campaigns, these notes to himself have guided readers for eighteen centuries. Timeless wisdom from a ruler who tried to live by philosophy.
timaeus: Plato's dialogue on the creation of the universe: the divine craftsman shapes order from chaos in a grand cosmic myth. The most influential cosmology before modern science, shaping thought for two thousand years. Philosophy reaching for the stars.
titus-andronicus: Shakespeare's goriest tragedy: the Roman general Titus takes revenge on Tamora the Goth queen in a spiral of mutilation and murder. Bloody beyond belief and thrillingly theatrical, it was his first hit. Not for the squeamish, but impossible to forget.
toby-tyler-or-ten-weeks-with-a-circus: James Otis' immortal Toby Tyler — ten weeks with a circus — follows the runaway boy through sawdust and spangles to hard-won wisdom. The classic American circus story for children. Every child's favorite since 1881, and still going strong. The skeleton, the fat lady, and kind Mr. Stubbs live in memory.
un-un-res-first-report-on-the-united-nat:
Cyprus got a United Nations peacekeeping force in 1964, and this first report on the force records its early days. Fighting between Greek Cypriot and Turkish Cypriot groups had pushed the island toward war. The Security Council sent the force, UNFICYP, to keep the peace and restore calm.

The report describes the force's arrival, its patrols, and its talks with both sides. It covers early clashes, blocked roads, and efforts to return life to normal. Nobody then guessed the force would still be on the island decades later. The report is the opening page of that long story.
un-un-res-second-report-on-the-united-na:
A second report on the United Nations Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus follows the force through its first months in 1964. UNFICYP had arrived that spring to stop fighting between the island's Greek and Turkish communities. The calm it guarded was thin, and armed posts still faced each other in many towns.

The report describes patrol work, local truces, and efforts to reopen roads and markets. It also covers the force's talks with both leaderships about limits on armed men. The text shows a young mission learning its trade, and an island settling into a division that would last.
